blocks.text: In the introduction we learned what a deque is. Now let us get hands on with what you can actually do with one.
A deque exposes a small, clean set of operations. Once you know these six, you know the entire interface. Everything else is just built on top of them.
The magic of a deque is that every one of these operations runs in O(1). No matter how large the deque grows, each call does a fixed amount of work.
Two operations add an element. Two remove one. The only choice you make is which end you work on.

items: Push front: add an element to the front
Push back: add an element to the back
Pop front: remove and return the front element
Pop back: remove and return the back element

blocks.text: Here are the real method names in the three most common interview languages:

codes.java:
Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();

dq.addFirst(x);   // push front
dq.addLast(x);    // push back
dq.pollFirst();   // pop front
dq.pollLast();    // pop back
codes.python:
from collections import deque
dq = deque()

dq.appendleft(x)  # push front
dq.append(x)      # push back
dq.popleft()      # pop front
dq.pop()          # pop back
codes.cpp:
deque<int> dq;

dq.push_front(x); // push front
dq.push_back(x);  // push back
dq.pop_front();   // pop front
dq.pop_back();    // pop back

Sometimes you want to look at an element without removing it, or simply ask how many items the deque holds.

items: Peek front: read the front element and leave it in place
Peek back: read the back element and leave it in place
Is empty: true when there are no elements

blocks.text: Always check that the deque is not empty before you pop or peek. Calling these on an empty deque is one of the most common bugs in interviews.

codes.java:
dq.peekFirst();   // look at the front
dq.peekLast();    // look at the back
dq.size();        // number of elements
dq.isEmpty();     // true when empty
codes.python:
dq[0]             # look at the front
dq[-1]            # look at the back
len(dq)           # number of elements
not dq            # True when empty
codes.cpp:
dq.front();       // look at the front
dq.back();        // look at the back
dq.size();        // number of elements
dq.empty();       // true when empty

blocks.text: This is the headline feature of a deque, so it is worth stating clearly. Every core operation is constant time:

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Time Complexity"],"rows":[["Push front / push back","O(1)"],["Pop front / pop back","O(1)"],["Peek front / peek back","O(1)"],["Size / is empty","O(1)"],["Access a middle element","O(n), not what it is for"]]}

blocks.text: Notice what is missing. There is no fast way to reach into the middle of a deque. Looking up the element at some arbitrary index is not what a deque is for. If you need that, an array or a list is the better tool.
Use a deque when all the action happens at the two ends. The moment you need random access to the middle, reach for something else.
You do not need to build a deque yourself, but understanding how it works under the hood helps you trust the O(1) promise. There are two classic ways to build one.
Approach 1: Doubly Linked List

Each node holds a value plus a pointer to the node before it and the node after it. The deque keeps a reference to both the head and the tail, so adding or removing at either end is just a few pointer updates. That is always O(1).
Approach 2: Circular Array

A fixed size array is used like a ring, with two markers for the front and the back. When a marker runs off one edge, it wraps around to the other side. This avoids shifting elements, so every operation stays O(1) as long as the array has room.
Most standard libraries use a growable circular array because it is cache friendly and fast in practice. Java ArrayDeque is a great example of this.
The best way to lock in these operations is to build a deque yourself. These two problems ask you to do exactly that:

items: Design Circular Deque: implement a deque on top of a fixed size circular array.
Design Front Middle Back Queue: a twist that also supports inserting and removing in the middle.

Once these operations feel automatic, you are ready for the fun part: the clever problems a deque can solve. That is the applications lesson.
